chapter: Riverboat to New Orleans and Horace Henderson
title: Staying with his wife's aunt in Cleveland and going home in defeat
summary: He and Granger stayed at his wife's aunt's home in Cleveland, doing dishes in exchange for greens and ribs; then they wired home for fare and returned, hearing that he should have gone to college.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: So nothing happened for us in Buffalo, because in the first place he was in a big hurry to get away. He wanted to go back home. He didn't have no eyes for that. So I said, "Well, we'll go back to Cleveland." See the only reason I wanted to go back to Cleveland was because my wife's aunt had a home there, and out of Horace's band, me and Granger and Elizabeth's brother-in-law, who was -- her nephew, you know.
So we didn't have no trouble, you know.
We stayed there, yeah. She didn't even want you to eat. You know, you were brought up different. You wouldn't sponge off her. It was enough sleeping there, you know.

So sometimes she used to make us eat by saying -- leaving a note that said, 'Jonah, I had to go downtown, so I'd appreciate it very much if you fellows would clean out the pots and pans and wash the dishes for me, because I might be late getting home and I want to cook.' We would jump in there, man, and eat them greens and barbecued ribs, throwing that stuff out. So it's funny how things happen to you, if you try.

Now, a lot of people will come to your rescue if you try, you know. I've always had a belief they'll help you along. So -- of course I didn't want to wear it out, you know, and I didn't blame Granger, because -- but he said, 'Well, it's all right for you and Russell, but for me, I can't make it. I won't do it.' And I don't want to stay out here unless he -- unless he's with me, you know, because we're buddies, you know. We've gone everywhere together, we've come up as kids

together. So now he sends home for money. So I have to send home for money, the fare back. So they sent me my fare, so we went on back. But I wasn't satisfied. I was very unhappy, and then they said, "See, why didn't you go to school like we told you? See what happens?" I knew I was going to get that, you know, because if it had been left to me I'd have stayed in Cleveland or Buffalo and made it --
-- some kind of way, you know.
Now you had the problem of how to get away again.
